On the US side, Ebury does not expect the Fed to move rates at all this year, viewing the inflation situation as less severe than feared. The US labor market is showing signs of stabilization rather than weakness or strength, which does not support the case for rate hikes in the near term.
quote: In terms of our, I guess, the next 3 to 4 months for the end of the year, we do expect it to trade a bit of a tight range, um, with the with the US dollar. We expect it to end the year around at about 71 US cents. Um, that's likely or that's largely driven by one the RBA retaining its hawkish bias, though there are still some upside risk on the inflation outlook at least. And then on the fed as well. As I flagged earlier, we don't think the fed will be moving rates at all this year. We think that the inflation story, um, isn't as bad as as feared. And so when you look at the labor market over there, we wouldn't say it's weak, but we wouldn't say it's necessarily strong. headline: Ebury Partners expects RBA to remain on hold until mid-2024, citing softening spending and lagged rate hike impact
reasoning: Malouf notes the RBA held rates unanimously and that Governor Bullock's post-decision comments were relatively hawkish, flagging that further rate rises remain possible. However, Ebury's view is that the RBA does not need to raise further, as data since the June meeting has come in below the RBA's inflation expectations and the unemployment rate has risen above their forecasts. The RBA has modestly downgraded near-term inflation forecasts and upgraded unemployment forecasts. Malouf believes the correction in house prices will naturally soften consumer spending in the second half of the year, and the full lagged impact of recent rate hikes has not yet been felt by mortgage holders. He expects the RBA to remain on hold at least until mid-next year.
quote: In our view, we just don't think that they need to be moving rates any further. Uh, we think the the deterioration or the deterioration probably a bit too strong, but the correction that we are seeing in house prices across the country, uh, will naturally see, uh, spending soften, at least in the second half of this year. We don't think the full impact of the, uh, of the recent rate hikes have been truly felt. Yet there's generally a bit of a lag between when rate rises happened from the RBA and when they actually felt by mortgage holders. So we think the second half of this year, we're going to see a bit of a softening in spending. Uh, and then on top of that, just other areas of the economy are showing some pockets of, of weakening. And that naturally should keep inflation in check in our view. And that's why we think the RBA will remain on hold at least until the middle of next year.

headline: Ebury Partners sees US core inflation cooling on 3-month basis, supporting Fed on-hold stance through year-end
reasoning: Anthony Malouf notes that US core inflation on a three-month annualised basis has fallen to 1.6%, which he views as a promising signal for the Fed's rate decision. Core goods prices rose only 0.2% in the month, suggesting tariff-related cost pressures are not feeding through as severely as feared. Shelter inflation, the largest CPI component, rose just 0.1%, and Zillow asking rents data shows rents in some US states are actually falling. Malouf expects this to put downward pressure on headline inflation over the next 6-12 months. His base case is that the Fed will remain on hold for the rest of the year with no rate moves.
quote: The data did come in line with expectations. I think one thing worth highlighting is that if you look at things on a three month annualized basis, at least for core inflation, um, a core inflation on a three month annualized basis is now at 1.6%. So that's quite a promising, uh, read, at least, um, for the for for our rate call decision for the fed. Um, on top of that, you know, core goods prices there were only up 0.2% through the month. So no real signs that, you know, higher tariffs and elevated costs, in particular for things like chips related to data centers, aren't really feeding through as severely as maybe previously anticipated. Um, and on top of that, we did say shelter, which is the largest component of us CPI. It was only up a modest 0.1%. And rents, which make up a large portion of that. Um, when you look at higher frequency measures, such as the Zillow asking rents, it's actually showing that asking rents in some states in the US are actually falling. So in our view, we actually think this will put some downward pressure on on headline inflation, at least in the next 6 to 12 months. And it supports our view that we don't think the fed will move rates at all this year, and they'll remain on hold.
